question: What main data structures do you know?
answer:
Data structures are specialized formats for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data efficiently. They are broadly categorized into:

1. Linear Data Structures

  • Arrays: Fixed-size contiguous memory blocks allowing $O(1)$ random access.
  • Dynamic Arrays / Vectors: Resizable contiguous arrays with amortized $O(1)$ appends.
  • Linked Lists: Nodes with pointers (Singly, Doubly, Circular); efficient $O(1)$ insertions/deletions at known positions.
  • Stacks: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) structures with push/pop operations.
  • Queues: FIFO (First-In, First-Out) structures, including Deques and Priority Queues.

2. Non-Linear Data Structures

  • Trees: Hierarchical structures (Binary Trees, BSTs, Self-Balancing Trees like AVL and Red-Black Trees, B/B+ Trees, Tries, Heaps).
  • Graphs: Vertices and edges representing networks (directed/undirected, cyclic/acyclic, weighted/unweighted).

3. Hash-Based & Associative Structures

  • Hash Tables / Maps / Sets: Key-value stores using hash functions for expected $O(1)$ lookups.
  • Bitsets / Bloom Filters: Space-efficient probabilistic or compact bitwise containers.

question: What is the difference between singly linked list and doubly linked list data structures?
answer:
Both are node-based linear collections, but differ in pointer links, directional traversals, and memory footprint:

  • Singly Linked List (SLL): Each node contains the data and a single pointer (next) pointing to the successor node. Traversal is strictly unidirectional (head to tail).
  • Doubly Linked List (DLL): Each node contains the data and two pointers: next and prev. Traversal is bidirectional (forward and backward).
DimensionSingly Linked ListDoubly Linked List
Pointers per Node1 pointer (next)2 pointers (next, prev)
Memory OverheadLower ($1 \times sizeof(pointer)$ per node)Higher ($2 \times sizeof(pointer)$ per node)
Deletion of Given Node$O(n)$ if predecessor is not given (must traverse to find previous node).$O(1)$ since predecessor is directly reachable via node->prev.
Reverse TraversalImpossible without auxiliary stack or reversing the list.Trivial and native ($O(1)$ per step backwards).
Implementation ComplexitySimple pointer manipulation.More complex (must update both next and prev safely).

question: What is the difference between stack and queue data structures?
answer:
Stacks and Queues are abstract linear data structures governed by different access and removal policies:

  • Stack (LIFO - Last In, First Out): The last element inserted is the first element to be removed. Insertions and removals occur at the same end (the top). Primary operations: push(x), pop(), peek() / top().
  • Queue (FIFO - First In, First Out): The first element inserted is the first element to be removed. Insertions occur at the back (rear / tail), and removals occur at the front (head). Primary operations: enqueue(x) / push(x), dequeue() / pop(), peek() / front().
FeatureStackQueue
PrincipleLIFO (Last In First Out)FIFO (First In First Out)
Access Points1 active end (Top)2 active ends (Front for removal, Rear for insertion)
Real-world AnalogyStack of cafeteria platesLine of people at a ticket counter
Primary Use CasesFunction call call-stack, recursion backtracking, undo/redo mechanics, bracket matching, DFS traversal.Task scheduling, message queues (RabbitMQ/Kafka), printer spoolers, BFS traversal, buffer caches.

question: What is algorithm complexity?
answer:
Algorithm Complexity is a formal mathematical measure of the computational resources (time and memory) required by an algorithm to execute as a function of the input size $n$.

1. Types of Complexity

  • Time Complexity: Quantifies the number of elementary operations executed by an algorithm relative to $n$.
  • Space Complexity: Quantifies the total memory consumed by an algorithm (auxiliary working space + input space) relative to $n$.

2. Asymptotic Notations

  • Big-O Notation ($O$): Represents the asymptotic upper bound (worst-case performance guarantee). It describes the maximum growth rate as $n \to \infty$.
  • Big-Omega Notation ($\Omega$): Represents the asymptotic lower bound (best-case performance).
  • Big-Theta Notation ($\Theta$): Represents an asymptotically tight bound where upper and lower bounds match ($f(n) = \Theta(g(n))$).

3. Common Complexity Hierarchy

$$O(1) < O(\log n) < O(\sqrt{n}) < O(n) < O(n \log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!)$$

question: What are associative unordered and ordered containers?
answer:
Associative containers store elements as key-value pairs (or unique keys) enabling fast lookup by key rather than index.

1. Ordered Associative Containers

  • Underlying Structure: Self-balancing Binary Search Trees (typically Red-Black Trees).
  • Ordering: Strict weak ordering maintained according to a comparator (default: <). Iteration traverses elements in sorted order.
  • Time Complexity: Search, Insert, and Delete are guaranteed $O(\log n)$.
  • Standard Implementations: C++ std::map / std::set; C# SortedDictionary<K,V> / SortedSet<T>.

2. Unordered Associative Containers

  • Underlying Structure: Hash Table (array of buckets with hash collision chaining or open addressing).
  • Ordering: No predictable order; iteration sequence depends on bucket distribution and hash values.
  • Time Complexity: Average case $O(1)$ for Search, Insert, and Delete; worst case $O(n)$ (when hash collisions degrade buckets into linear chains).
  • Standard Implementations: C++ std::unordered_map / std::unordered_set; Python dict / set; C# Dictionary<K,V> / HashSet<T>.

question: Explain what the binary tree is.
answer:
A Binary Tree is a hierarchical non-linear data structure composed of nodes, where each node has at most two children, conventionally referred to as the left child and right child.

Key Properties & Terminology

  • Root: The topmost node with no parent.
  • Leaf Node: A node with zero children.
  • Depth / Height: The length of the path from root to node (depth) or from node to deepest leaf (height).
  • Max nodes at level $l$: $2^l$ (assuming root is level 0).
  • Max nodes in tree of height $h$: $2^{h+1} - 1$.

Special Types of Binary Trees

  • Full Binary Tree: Every node has either 0 or 2 children.
  • Complete Binary Tree: All levels are completely filled except possibly the last level, which is populated left-to-right (used in Binary Heaps).
  • Perfect Binary Tree: All internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are at the exact same level.
  • Binary Search Tree (BST): For every node $N$, all nodes in its left subtree have keys $\le N.key$, and all nodes in its right subtree have keys $\ge N.key$.
  • Balanced Binary Tree (e.g., AVL, Red-Black): Enforces height constraints such that height remains $O(\log n)$.

question: What is the search time complexity for binary tree? Why? Is it guaranteed?
answer:
The search time complexity depends directly on whether the tree is a generic binary tree, an arbitrary Binary Search Tree (BST), or a self-balancing BST:

1. Unordered Binary Tree

  • Time Complexity: $O(n)$. Because no ordering property exists, every single node must be inspected via BFS or DFS in the worst case.

2. Standard Binary Search Tree (BST)

  • Average Case: $O(\log n)$. When keys are inserted in random order, height is balanced on average, halving the search space at each branch.
  • Worst Case: $O(n)$. If elements are inserted in already sorted or reverse-sorted order (e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), the tree degenerates into a linear linked list (skewed tree) of height $n$.

3. Is $O(\log n)$ Guaranteed?

No, it is NOT guaranteed in a basic BST.

To guarantee $O(\log n)$ search time, you must use Self-Balancing Binary Search Trees such as AVL Trees or Red-Black Trees, which perform tree rotations on insertions and deletions to strictly maintain a height bound of $h \le c \cdot \log_2 n$.

question: What is the structure of a hash table? How does it work?
answer:
A Hash Table is a data structure that implements an associative array abstract data type, mapping keys to values using a Hash Function.

1. Core Components

  • Underlying Array (Buckets): A contiguous block of memory slots of size $M$.
  • Hash Function: A mathematical function $h(k)$ converting an arbitrary key $k$ into an integer hash code, mapped to an array index via $index = h(k) \pmod M$.
  • Collision Resolution Strategy: Mechanism to handle cases where two distinct keys produce the same index.

2. How Collision Resolution Works

  • Separate Chaining: Each bucket holds a linked list (or balanced tree if bucket length grows large, as in Java 8+ HashMap). Colliding keys are appended to the bucket's list.
  • Open Addressing: All elements reside directly in the bucket array. Upon collision, systematic probing is performed to find the next empty slot:
    • Linear Probing: $index = (h(k) + i) \pmod M$
    • Quadratic Probing: $index = (h(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) \pmod M$
    • Double Hashing: $index = (h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \pmod M$

3. Load Factor and Dynamic Resizing

The Load Factor is $\alpha = \frac{N}{M}$ ($N$ = items, $M$ = capacity). When $\alpha$ exceeds a predefined threshold (typically $0.70$–$0.75$), the array is resized (typically doubled), and all existing elements are rehashed to maintain constant-time performance.

question: What is the time complexity of add/search operations in a hash table?
answer:
The time complexity of insertion (add), search (lookup), and deletion operations in a hash table depends on the collision frequency and load factor:

OperationAverage CaseWorst CaseExplanation
Search (Lookup)$O(1)$$O(n)$Uniform hashing distributes keys evenly across buckets. In the worst case (all keys hash to the identical bucket), lookup degrades to traversing a linked list of length $n$.
Add (Insertion)$O(1)$ (amortized)$O(n)$Inserting into an existing bucket takes $O(1)$. When load factor threshold is breached, resizing allocates a new array and rehashes all $n$ items ($O(n)$ spike, amortizing to $O(1)$).
Delete$O(1)$$O(n)$Finding the key takes $O(1)$ average, followed by pointer relinking.

Note: In modern libraries (like Java 8+ HashMap), worst-case search is improved from $O(n)$ to $O(\log n)$ by converting overloaded buckets into Red-Black Trees when bucket size exceeds 8.

question: Explain what the binary search algorithm is.
answer:
Binary Search is an optimal search algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half (Divide and Conquer).

How It Works

  1. Initialize two pointers: low = 0 and high = n - 1.
  2. Calculate the midpoint: mid = low + (high - low) / 2 (preventing integer overflow).
  3. Compare target with array element at mid:
    • If arr[mid] == target: Target found; return mid.
    • If arr[mid] < target: Target must be in the right half; set low = mid + 1.
    • If arr[mid] > target: Target must be in the left half; set high = mid - 1.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until low > high. If not found, return $-1$.

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(\log n)$ (reduces search space by factor of 2 at each iteration: $\frac{n}{2^k} = 1 \implies k = \log_2 n$).
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$ iterative, $O(\log n)$ recursive (due to call stack).
  • Prerequisite: Data container must be sorted and support $O(1)$ random access.

# Quick Sort implementation
def quick_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1: return arr
    pivot = arr[len(arr) // 2]
    left = [x for x in arr if x < pivot]
    mid = [x for x in arr if x == pivot]
    right = [x for x in arr if x > pivot]
    return quick_sort(left) + mid + quick_sort(right)

question: How do you effectively delete sequence of elements from the middle of array?
answer:
Deleting a contiguous sequence of $k$ elements starting at index $start$ ($[start, start + k - 1]$) from an array of size $n$ can be done effectively in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space:

Optimal Approach: In-Place Shifting (Memmove / Two-Pointers)

  1. Shift all subsequent elements located at indices from $start + k$ through $n - 1$ to the left by $k$ positions: arr[i] = arr[i + k].
  2. Truncate the logical size of the array or resize the container by $k$ elements.
  3. Using low-level memory block movement (memmove or std::move) minimizes overhead by moving blocks of raw bytes via SIMD/cache lines rather than element-by-element manual loops.

Complexity: Time: $O(n - start - k)$ elements shifted (at most $O(n)$); Space: $O(1)$ in-place.

code_snippets.python:
def delete_sequence(arr, start, k):
    """Deletes k elements starting from index start in-place."""
    # Slice assignment in Python shifts underlying C-array efficiently via memmove
    arr[start:start + k] = []
    return arr

# Example:
a = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
delete_sequence(a, 2, 3) # Removes 2, 3, 4 -> [0, 1, 5, 6, 7]

question: Given an array with 100 elements (numbers from 0 to 99). One element has been removed from the array. How would you find the removed element? How would you solve this if the array is sorted, or the array is not sorted?
answer:
The original set consists of all integers in the range $[0, 99]$ (total $N = 100$ numbers). The array currently contains 99 distinct elements with 1 number missing.

Case 1: The Array is NOT Sorted

  • Method A: Mathematical Sum ($O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space)
    The expected sum of numbers from $0$ to $N - 1$ is $\frac{(N - 1) \times N}{2} = \frac{99 \times 100}{2} = 4950$.
    The missing number is: $Missing = 4950 - \sum_{i=0}^{98} arr[i]$.
  • Method B: XOR Accumulation ($O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space, No Overflow risk)
    Compute $XOR = (0 \oplus 1 \oplus \dots \oplus 99) \oplus (arr[0] \oplus \dots \oplus arr[98])$. Because $x \oplus x = 0$ and $x \oplus 0 = x$, all paired elements cancel out, leaving exactly the missing number.

Case 2: The Array IS Sorted

  • Method: Modified Binary Search ($O(\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ space)
    Since numbers are originally $0, 1, \dots, 99$, before the missing element, each element matches its index: arr[i] == i.
    At and after the missing element, indices shift: arr[i] == i + 1.
    We binary search for the first index where arr[mid] != mid. That index is the missing number.

question: How do you find duplicates in array? How would you solve it for the array of chars?
answer:
Finding duplicates can be approached in multiple ways depending on memory constraints and value range:

1. General Array of Elements

  • Hash Set ($O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space): Iterate through elements, inserting into a HashSet. If set.contains(x) is true, $x$ is a duplicate.
  • Sorting ($O(n \log n)$ time, $O(1)$ auxiliary space): Sort the array and check adjacent elements: arr[i] == arr[i-1].
  • In-place Negation (if elements are bounded in $[1, n]$): Use values as indices and negate the value at arr[abs(x) - 1]. If already negative, $x$ is a duplicate ($O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space).

2. Specialized Solution for Array of char

  • Direct Addressing / Fixed Frequency Array ($O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space):
    Since the ASCII character set has only 128 (or 256 for extended ASCII) possibilities, use a fixed-size boolean or integer array: bool seen[256] = {false};.
    Space is strictly constant: exactly 256 bytes regardless of input size $n$.
  • Bit Manipulation (Bitmask) ($O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space, 8–32 bytes memory):
    If characters are restricted to lowercase English letters ('a'–'z'), a single 32-bit integer bitmask can track occurrences using checker & (1 << (c - 'a')).

question: How do you find the middle element of a singly linked list in one pass?
answer:
The optimal technique to find the middle element of a singly linked list in a single pass is the Fast and Slow Pointer (Tortoise and Hare) algorithm:

Algorithm Steps

  1. Initialize two pointers, slow and fast, both pointing to the head of the linked list.
  2. Traverse the list: in each step, advance slow by 1 node and fast by 2 nodes.
  3. Continue while fast != null && fast.next != null.
  4. When fast reaches the end (or runs off the end), slow will be positioned exactly at the middle element.

Even vs Odd Lengths

  • Odd length ($2k + 1$ nodes): When fast.next == null, slow points to the exact middle node (node $k + 1$).
  • Even length ($2k$ nodes): When fast == null, slow points to the second middle node (node $k + 1$). If the first middle node is required, terminate when fast.next.next == null.

Complexity: Time: $O(n)$ (traverses the list exactly once); Space: $O(1)$ auxiliary space.

question: How do you detect a loop in a singly linked list?
answer:
The industry-standard optimal approach is Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm (also known as the Tortoise and Hare algorithm):

1. Cycle Detection Principle

  1. Initialize two pointers at head: slow (moves 1 step at a time) and fast (moves 2 steps at a time).
  2. Advance both pointers until fast or fast.next becomes null (no cycle) or slow == fast (cycle detected).
  3. If a cycle exists, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer inside the loop because the relative distance between them decreases by 1 node per iteration ($2 - 1 = 1$).

2. Finding the Start of the Loop (Follow-up)

Once slow == fast, reset slow = head while keeping fast at the meeting point. Move both pointers forward 1 step at a time. The node where they meet again is the exact start of the cycle ($L_{head\_to\_cycle} = k \cdot C - d_{entry\_to\_meet}$).

Complexity: Time: $O(n)$; Auxiliary Space: $O(1)$.

question: Given an array of numbers: 20, 17, 30, 21, 45, 2, 18. Form a sorted binary tree diagram. How should the sequences be changed to produce the worst binary search tree?
answer:
Given the insertion sequence: [20, 17, 30, 21, 45, 2, 18] into a Binary Search Tree (BST):

1. Step-by-Step BST Construction

  1. 20: Root node.
  2. 17: $17 < 20 \implies$ Left child of 20.
  3. 30: $30 > 20 \implies$ Right child of 20.
  4. 21: $21 > 20, 21 < 30 \implies$ Left child of 30.
  5. 45: $45 > 20, 45 > 30 \implies$ Right child of 30.
  6. 2: $2 < 20, 2 < 17 \implies$ Left child of 17.
  7. 18: $18 < 20, 18 > 17 \implies$ Right child of 17.

Tree Diagram:

        20
       /  \
     17    30
    /  \   /  \
   2   18 21   45

Note: This resulting tree is a balanced, complete binary search tree of minimum height $h = 2$ (levels 0, 1, 2).

2. Sequence to Produce the Worst BST

The worst possible BST is a degenerate (skewed) tree where every node has only one child, forming an effective linked list with maximum height $h = n - 1 = 6$ and $O(n)$ search time.

To produce this worst BST, the sequence must be inserted in strictly monotonically sorted order:

  • Right-skewed worst sequence (Ascending): [2, 17, 18, 20, 21, 30, 45] (every node inserted to the right child).
  • Left-skewed worst sequence (Descending): [45, 30, 21, 20, 18, 17, 2] (every node inserted to the left child).

question: Provide a recursive and a non-recursive solution for the tree traversal algorithms for a binary tree.
answer:
Tree traversal visits every node in a binary tree exactly once. The three classic depth-first traversals are Pre-order (Root, L, R), In-order (L, Root, R), and Post-order (L, R, Root).

1. In-Order Traversal (L $\to$ Root $\to$ R)

  • Recursive: Trivially call inorder(node.left), process node.val, then call inorder(node.right).
  • Iterative (Non-recursive): Uses an explicit Stack. Push nodes moving as far left as possible. When left reaches null, pop from stack, visit the node, and transition to its right child.

2. Pre-Order Traversal (Root $\to$ L $\to$ R)

  • Recursive: Process node.val, then recurse left and right.
  • Iterative: Push root to stack. In each loop iteration, pop node, visit it, and push right child first, then left child (ensuring left is processed first due to LIFO).

Complexity: Time: $O(n)$ for all approaches. Auxiliary Space: $O(h)$ where $h$ is tree height.

code_snippets.python:
# Recursive In-Order
def inorder_recursive(root):
    res = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        dfs(node.left)
        res.append(node.val)
        dfs(node.right)
    dfs(root)
    return res

# Non-Recursive (Iterative) In-Order
def inorder_iterative(root):
    res, stack, curr = [], [], root
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        res.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.right
    return res
